content.thinking:
I notice the logs show the flag remained "on" even after the revert attempt, meaning the errors kept happening — so the real issue is that the revert didn't actually take effect, not that the fix was wrong. I need to be careful to flag the root cause as strongly suggested but unconfirmed: likely a ZeroDivisionError in spend_summary.py around line 47, triggered on a path gated by the monthly-related flag, and I shouldn't restate any impact numbers as if they were verified.

For the executive summary, I'll keep it component-agnostic — account and spending pages on the shop, roughly a third of requests failing starting 21:43 UTC, still unresolved 11 minutes later when it went to humans after the automated fix attempt failed. I'll avoid presenting any cost or error-rate figures as my own calculation, framing them instead as reported metrics with qualifiers like "roughly" or "a large fraction," and I'll close with a clear list of assumptions.

assumptions: That the incident began at 21:43 UTC — this is the automated responder's placement of onset from the metric series, consistent with the first ZeroDivisionError in the logs, not an independently confirmed start time.
That customer impact was confined to the account page — inferred from the log lines read, which only cover account-page requests; no other endpoints were examined.
That the failing requests were genuine customer-visible failures rather than retried or degraded-but-served responses; no client-side or downstream confirmation was gathered.

That the flag revert issued at 21:49 was actually applied. The flag-evaluation logs continued to report the feature as on afterwards, so it is equally possible the revert never took effect. This was not verified against the flag provider after the action.
That the incident was still unresolved at escalation — the metrics window simply ends at 21:52/21:53, so recovery after that point is unknown, not ruled out.
That this incident shares a cause with the earlier matched incident 9c1d4e7a-0000-4000-8000-00000000fee1; the match came from similarity in memory, and the two were not compared in detail.
input.executive_summary: Starting at 21:43 UTC on 28 September 2026, a substantial share of customer account-page requests on the online shop began failing outright — the reported error rate for the period sat around 30% of requests, against a roughly 1% baseline, peaking near 40%. Shoppers hitting their account page would have seen an error instead of their spending summary; checkout and other pages were not implicated in the evidence reviewed. The trigger coincided with a new spending-summary feature being switched on for customers. The automated responder picked up the alert at 21:48, identified the feature switch within a minute, and turned it back off at 21:49. The failures did not stop. After waiting three minutes and confirming no improvement, the responder handed the incident to a human on-call at 21:53. The service had not recovered by the last minute of data available, so the outage lasted at least eleven minutes and was still ongoing at handover; the true duration and customer impact are larger than the figures above, which are lower bounds, not final measurements. The one remedy attempted did not work, and the fault was unresolved at the time of escalation.
input.root_cause: Unconfirmed at escalation. The evidence points to the account-page code path gated by the `monthly-spend-feature` flag: the flag went from all-off to a partial rollout at 21:43 and fully on at 21:44, and from 21:43 onward the error logs are dominated by `ZeroDivisionError: division by zero at src/io_shop/spend_summary.py:47`, with latency percentiles flat (an error-path fault, not saturation). However, the one mitigation attempted — reverting `monthly-spend-feature` at 21:49 — did not restore baseline: flag-evaluation log lines continued to report the feature as on through 21:52 and the ZeroDivisionErrors continued at the same rate, so the revert either did not take effect (stuck rollout state or cached evaluations) or the flag toggle is correlated with, rather than the sole cause of, the failure. The same flag revert had already failed to resolve a prior matching incident (9c1d4e7a-0000-4000-8000-00000000fee1). A human owner needs to confirm whether the flag state actually changed and fix the division-by-zero in the spend-summary calculation regardless.
